# Thanks to Xander!



* Quick thanks to Xander for running our second SPOTLIGHT lecture on “What methods and ethics of inquiry are used in linguistics research?”
  * Ethics
    * It’s ultimately about doing no harm – that’s what makes the Milgram Experiment unethical\!
    * Linguists also have to consider harm – how is the “danger of death” question potentially harmful?
    * You need consent\, data plan\, minimal risk\, necessary data only\, and accountability
  * Methods
    * Sociology research = similar to linguistics research\!
    * Linguists conduct experiments\, collect survey data\, go to communities to be participant observers\, and use existing resources as ways to collect data to help them answer their research questions

# What is language acquisition?



* __Language acquisition __ is the process by which humans acquire the ability to use\, produce\, and perceive language\!
  * Involves the acquisition of all functional aspects of the system\, including syntax\, morphology\, phonology\, lexicon\, etc\.
* __First Language Acquisition: __ how an infant acquires his/her first or native language
* __Second Language Acquisition: __ how children and adults acquire additional languages beyond the first

Early research suggested that language learning was a process of  __induction__

Children generalize linguistic patterns from the input they receive

inference of a generalized conclusion from particular instances; compare deduction

# Acquiring a First Language


---


# Hypothesis #2: Innateness



* __The Innateness Hypothesis__
  * Language  _ability_  in humans is  __innate__ \, or inborn
  * Humans are genetically predisposed to learn/use language
  * Babies are born with the knowledge that languages have patterns and with the ability to seek out those patterns
  * Requires reinforcement\, but no one “teaches” you how to talk
    * Children learn language as they live in it
    * But acquiring language is more than memorizing words and phrases
    * Grammatical and communicative competence
  * We need induction  _and _ innateness to handle language acquisition

---


![](images/13-How%20do%20kids%20learn%20to%20talk_5.jpg)

# If it’s built in, why aren’t we born talking?!



* Beyond physical  __maturation__ \, there are  __two __ other aspects of maturation crucial to a child’s ability to acquire a language:
* __Symbolization__
  * Language = symbolic = arbitrary representation of the world
  * To acquire language\, a child must be able to keep a mental picture of an absent object
* __Using tools__
  * Language = a tool that gets work done
  * Children begin using language in this way purposefully to get things they can’t get physically

how do adults interact with babies to  _facilitate_  the language acquisition process?

![](images/13-How%20do%20kids%20learn%20to%20talk_6.png)

# Baby Talk

__Baby talk__  is a register that adults use to talk to younger children

Not all cultures use Baby Talk

Children learn language at same rate\!

But it’s clear that it must serve some purpose\, otherwise so many groups would have begun to use it nor continue to use it\!

::: {.notes}

Exaggerated prosody helps children acquire phonology more easily
Simplified sentences help children acquire syntax more easily

:::

# One-Word Stage: 12 months

Children often overgeneralize with these words

![](images/13-How%20do%20kids%20learn%20to%20talk_8.png)

![](images/13-How%20do%20kids%20learn%20to%20talk_9.png)

![](images/13-How%20do%20kids%20learn%20to%20talk_10.png)


---




* Research suggests that children are doing more than just rehearsing single words
  * Children use single words to express whole propositions
  * A child may say “Dada” to mean different things in different contexts
* “Dada”


Here comes Daddy\!

This is for Daddy\.

That is where Daddy sits\.

This shoe is Daddy’s\.


---


# Two-Word Stage: 1 ½ years

![](images/13-How%20do%20kids%20learn%20to%20talk_11.png)



* The child has about 50 words in his/her vocabulary
* Utterances typically contain one noun\-like subject element and one predicate\-like element
  * Something like “John apple” is like…
  * _John_  	 _ate an apple_
  * subject       predicate

---


![](images/13-How%20do%20kids%20learn%20to%20talk_12.jpg)

# Beyond two words?



* Here is a real parent\-child \(2;8\) interaction:
  * Child: I beed a princess\.
  * Mommy: You are the princess?
  * Child: No\, I  __beed__  a princess\.
* What happened?
  * Sounds Mommy heard: \[ajbidəprɪncɛs\]
    * Mommy’s interpretation = “I be \(am\) the princess”
    * Mommy questions child about utterance
  * Child’s actual meaning = “I beed \(was\) a princess”
    * Child has overgeneralized regular past tense
